thread.title: Why Walgreens, not GE, could suffer the ‘Curse of the Dow’ - MarketWatch

author: Gary Smith
title: Why Walgreens, not GE, could suffer the ‘Curse of the Dow’ - MarketWatch
text:
General Electric is out; Walgreens Boots Alliance is in. When this switch to the Dow Jones Industrial Average was announced on Tuesday, many commentators predicted that it would give Walgreens stock a boost, as investors who buy Dow stocks would buy more Walgreens.
It doesn’t usually work that way. A more likely outcome is that Walgreens WBA, -0.78% not GE, -1.71% will suffer the Curse of the Dow.
A study I did with two of my students a few years ago looked at every change in the Dow DJIA, -0.65% back to October 1, 1928, when the Dow expanded to 30 stocks. We compared the performance of an Addition portfolio, consisting of stocks added to the Dow over the years, with the performance of a Deletion portfolio, consisting of the stocks that were replaced. The Deletion portfolio beat the Addition portfolio by about four percentage points a year — a huge difference compounded over decades.
This seems counter-intuitive, but actually makes perfect sense. A natural tendency in the stock market, where investors hope to invest in the next IBM IBM, -0.26% , Walmart WMT, -0.08% , or Apple AAPL, +0.36% , is to see a few years of rapidly increasing earnings and assume that many years of rapid growth lie ahead. However, corporate revenue and earnings fluctuate quarter-to-quarter and year-to-year in wild, unpredictable ways. The correlation between professional predictions of earnings changes and actual earnings changes is about 0.5 for predictions made three months into the current fiscal year. For predictions for the subsequent fiscal year, the correlation is 0.05. Accordingly, there’s a lot of luck in earnings.
A company with earnings up by 20% this year (or over the past few years), for example, is more likely to have experienced good luck than bad luck and, because luck is fleeting, its earnings will most likely regress towards the mean in the future, disappointing overly optimistic investors.
There is also regression for predicted earnings. The most optimistic earnings predictions are more likely to be overly rosy than to be excessively pessimistic, so the companies with the most optimistic forecasts usually don’t do as well as predicted. For instance, another study of mine looked at professional earnings predictions made in April for companies with December fiscal years. The companies were separated into quintiles based on their predicted percentage change in earnings.
The average predicted earnings increase for stocks in the top quintile was 1.2 standard deviations above the mean. Actual earnings turned out to be only 0.8 standard deviations above the mean. On the other end of the optimistic/pessimistic spectrum, the average predicted earnings increase for stocks in the bottom quintile was 1.2 standard deviations below the mean. Actual earnings turned out to be only 0.8 standard deviations below the mean.
Stock prices are likely to be too high for companies that are predicted to do well and too low for companies predicted to do poorly Put simply, stock prices are likely to be too high for companies that are predicted to do well and too low for companies predicted to do poorly — mistakes that will be corrected when earnings regress to the mean. If this conjecture is correct, stocks with relatively pessimistic earnings predictions may outperform stocks with relatively optimistic predictions. The average annual return for stock in the bottom earnings-prediction quintile was, in fact, two percentage points higher than for stocks in the top quintile.
Regarding Dow additions and deletions, the question for investors is not whether the companies going into the Dow are doing better than the companies they are replacing, but which stocks are better investments. The stocks going into and out of the Dow are all familiar companies that are closely watched. Investors are well-aware of the fact that Walgreens is doing great and GE is struggling. Their respective stock prices surely reflect this knowledge.
Yet the regression argument implies that the companies taken out of the Dow are generally not in as dire straits as their recent performance suggests, and that the companies replacing them are generally not as stellar as they appear. Companies doing wonderfully and predicted to do wonderfully usually disappoint, while the opposite is true of companies doing poorly.
If so, stock prices will often be unreasonably low for stocks going out of the Dow and undeservedly high for the stocks replacing them. When a company that is struggling regresses to the mean, its stock price will rise. When a company that is doing spectacularly regresses to the mean, its price will fall. This is why stocks booted out of the Dow so often outperform the stocks that replace them — the Curse of the Dow.
Walgreens is doing great and GE is doing poorly, but if you take regression into account, GE is likely the better investment .
Gary Smith is the Fletcher Jones Professor of Economics at Pomona College and author of “Money Machine: The Surprisingly Simple Power of Value Investing.”
